common.siteDescription: BUGTI Programmer Personality Test: understand how you share control, set rules, form judgments, and decide how much time to invest in code.

home.title: We all write code. What's your type?
home.description: BUGTI is a programmer personality test about your coding habits and technical preferences.
home.dimensionsDescription: See how the test distinguishes different approaches to code.
home.personalitiesDescription: From the Philosopher to the Doer, explore 16 different approaches to code.

dimensionsPage.title: What matters to you in a technical choice?
dimensionsPage.description: Control, constraints, cognition, and values describe how you make technical choices. One letter from each dimension forms a personality type.
dimensionsPage.pairsLabel: Four preference pairs in order: C/D, F/G, R/E, U/A

test.title: How do you like to write code?
test.description: Imagine facing 32 coding situations and answer based on your own preferences.
test.instructionExperience: Imagine facing each situation and choose how you would prefer to act. You can answer without prior experience; assume you could carry out either approach.
test.instructionChoice: Assume you have room to choose and time to decide. Both approaches must meet necessary correctness, security, compliance, and reliability requirements.
test.instructionHonesty: Choose what you would personally prefer, assuming your team allows either approach.
test.instructionNeutral: If you understand the situation but have no overall preference, choose Neutral. This answer counts toward your score.
test.reviewDescription: You can change any answer before viewing your result.
test.resumeNotice: Your unfinished answers are saved in this browser tab. You can reload and continue.
test.storageUnavailable: Your answers cannot be saved right now. You can keep answering, but reloading or closing this page will lose them.
test.leaveDescription: Your answers stay in this tab, so you can come back and continue.
test.linkInvalid: The answers in this link could not be restored. Please start a new test.

result.title: This link has no test result
result.description: Complete the test, then copy and save your result link to view your answers and result later.
result.invalidTitle: The result in this link could not be restored
result.invalidDescription: The link may be incomplete or come from an unsupported version. Copy the full original link or take the test again.
result.scoreExplanation: Each dimension uses scores from 0 to 100 to describe your preferences in these answers. The two scores add up to 100.
result.balancedTitle: Your answers fit more than one type
result.balancedDescription: At least one dimension has equal scores on both sides, so the result matches multiple types.
result.incompleteTitle: Some dimensions have too few answers
result.incompleteDescription: The earlier version's Cannot judge answers are not scored, leaving those dimensions without scores. Complete the current test to see all four dimensions.
result.answered: {count} of 8 answers count toward the score
result.nearBoundaryHelp: Changing answers could shift the preference to the other side.
result.copyFailed: Automatic copying failed. Copy the link from the field below.
result.shareDescription: The link contains your answers, and anyone with it can read them.
result.localLink: This is a local address that other people cannot open. Sharing requires the site to be deployed at an accessible address.
result.personalBreakdown: How you might make technical choices
result.allBalanced: Both sides have equal scores in all four dimensions. These answers show no overall preference.
result.patternBoth: On average, you agree with approaches on both sides.
result.patternNeither: On average, you disagree with approaches on both sides.
result.patternNeutral: Average agreement is neutral on both sides.
result.legacyNotice: This is a result from an earlier questionnaire. Its questions and scoring are unchanged. Take the current test to answer hypothetical situations.

about.description: Understand your preferences when making technical choices.
about.purpose: Programmers can approach the same technical problem differently. BUGTI asks which mechanisms you want to control, how much freedom you want, how you form judgments, and why you choose to spend more time on code.
about.limits: Your choices depend on the project, team, and experience. A four-letter type can help you reflect on your coding habits and discuss trade-offs with others.

constraints.title: Constraints
constraints.question: How much freedom do you keep, and which rules do you set upfront?

values.title: Values
values.question: What makes code worth more of your time?

cognition.title: Cognition
cognition.question: Where do you start when making a technical judgment?

C.label: Control
C.description: See how mechanisms work and adjust them yourself, accepting more complexity to keep control.

D.label: Delegation
D.description: Let reliable languages, frameworks, and platforms handle general mechanisms, leaving time for problems you need to solve yourself.

F.label: Flexibility
F.description: Keep room to combine and change things, accepting that developers will judge and verify some rules.

G.label: Guarantees
G.description: Put rules into types and models to restrict invalid states and operations upfront.

U.label: Utility
U.description: Weigh benefits, costs, and maintenance. Extra work needs a practical return.

A.label: Aesthetics
A.description: Value consistent structure and precise, elegant expression, even when better code has no immediate return.

R.label: Reasoning
R.description: Build a model first, then use its assumptions, causes, and limits to work out why a solution holds.

E.label: Experimentation
E.description: Start with a prototype or measurements, observe what happens, then revise your judgment.

typesPage.title: 16 ways to approach code
typesPage.description: Some prefer to ask why first; others like to try things. See how these types write code and which one feels like you.
typesPage.codeOrder: The order of the four-letter type code
typesPage.grouping: Start with Control (C) or Delegation (D). Control splits into CR and CE by Reasoning (R) or Experimentation (E). Delegation splits into DF and DG by Flexibility (F) or Guarantees (G). CR/CE use the first and third letters of the type code; DF/DG use the first two.

CR.title: Planners
CR.description: Keep control of key mechanisms. Think through principles, boundaries, and structure before putting the approach into practice.

CE.title: Practitioners
CE.description: Keep key mechanisms adjustable. Try them yourself to check effects and boundaries, then improve them based on feedback.

DF.title: Pioneers
DF.description: Use existing tools while keeping your approach flexible. Combine or replace tools to find what suits the goal.

DG.title: Guardians
DG.description: Leave general complexity to mature tools. Clear rules and guarantees handle repetitive details and help the parts work together reliably.

CFRU.name: Philosopher
CFRU.summary: Understand why first, then find a solution that makes sense and works.
CFRU.description: You tend to ask why and understand the key mechanisms before choosing a solution. Languages and techniques can vary, but the approach must make sense. Knowing the principles reduces guesswork and gives you more control over the implementation.
CFRU.inPractice: You may trace a mechanism, outline an approach, then change only the parts needed for the goal.
CFRU.watchFor: A convincing model can still miss a real condition. Small checks can help test its assumptions.
CFRU.collaboration: Explain the assumptions behind your choice and ask a hands-on teammate what to test first.

CFRA.name: Artist
CFRA.summary: Master the mechanisms so your code can express your own ideas.
CFRA.description: You see programming as a way to express ideas. You want control over the mechanisms and freedom to organize code in your own way. After the feature works, you still care whether the code expresses your intent accurately and has an elegant structure.
CFRA.inPractice: You may combine parts in your own way and refine the concepts until the code expresses your intent.
CFRA.watchFor: Organizing code around your own habits can make maintenance harder for others. Ask another maintainer to try following the structure.
CFRA.collaboration: Explain the idea behind the design and agree on which details are worth the shared time.

CFEU.name: Engineer
CFEU.summary: Adjust what you need and judge the tool by what it actually does.
CFEU.description: You treat programming as a tool for solving problems. You prefer to adjust key parts yourself and test the effects. Once the tool meets the need and the problem is solved, you usually stop investing solely in code quality.
CFEU.inPractice: You may inspect a problem, try a local change, and keep the solution that meets the need.
CFEU.watchFor: A local fix can affect other behavior. Check the surrounding interactions before finishing.
CFEU.collaboration: Provide a reproducible example and a clear result, then ask teammates to check which parts the change affects.

CFEA.name: Inventor
CFEA.summary: Try new possibilities yourself and build something clever that feels right.
CFEA.description: You enjoy trying things yourself and turning ideas into working code. With an existing implementation, you often keep testing changes or combinations. Discoveries make programming enjoyable and help you create something original that fits your idea.
CFEA.inPractice: You may experiment with mechanisms you can adjust and turn discoveries into an inventive implementation.
CFEA.watchFor: Continued experiments can expand the task. Agree on when to stop exploring and choose an approach.
CFEA.collaboration: Show an early prototype and separate essential discoveries from optional improvements.

CGRU.name: Goalkeeper
CGRU.summary: Understand the boundaries and stop avoidable problems before they happen.
CGRU.description: You first work out which behaviors the system should allow and which problems it should prevent. Then you put the rules into code you control. You are willing to prepare more to reduce surprises and make later problems easier to handle.
CGRU.inPractice: You may map failure paths and put key boundaries into code you maintain yourself.
CGRU.watchFor: Preventing every imagined problem may cost more than it saves. Focus on cases that are likely and have a large impact.
CGRU.collaboration: Explain the risk behind each rule and agree on which guarantees are needed now.

CGRA.name: Architect
CGRA.summary: Give every concept a place and every rule a reason in a consistent system.
CGRA.description: You want a clear, consistent system whose key mechanisms you can control. Each concept needs a precise place, and each rule needs a reason. Even when the system runs correctly, ambiguity, duplication, or contradictions make you want to reorganize the design.
CGRA.inPractice: You may check that the model, interfaces, and implementation agree and that each concept has a clear place.
CGRA.watchFor: Pursuing consistency can add changes before release. Agree on when the design is ready to ship.
CGRA.collaboration: Show the model and discuss which rules must stay consistent and which can be refined later.

CGEU.name: Inspector
CGEU.summary: A guarantee still needs a hands-on check before you trust it.
CGEU.description: You like explicit guarantees and prefer to check them yourself. You test boundaries, observe behavior, and adjust key details to confirm that the system works as expected under real conditions.
CGEU.inPractice: You may test explicit constraints and adjust the mechanisms where observations reveal a gap.
CGEU.watchFor: Passing tests only confirm the cases checked. Revisit the assumptions when the surrounding system changes.
CGEU.collaboration: Share boundary cases and distinguish what you observed from guarantees you have not yet tested.

CGEA.name: Craftsperson
CGEA.summary: Verify and refine by hand until correct work also feels well made.
CGEA.description: You want an implementation that follows clear rules, with care given to each detail. You like checking and adjusting it yourself. Even after the feature works correctly, you are willing to improve its behavior, structure, and expression.
CGEA.inPractice: You may repeatedly check and adjust an implementation until its behavior and expression agree.
CGEA.watchFor: You may want to keep refining after the practical need is met, so agree on completion criteria for the current iteration.
CGEA.collaboration: Use concrete examples in review and discuss correctness fixes separately from quality improvements.

DFRU.name: Planner
DFRU.summary: Plan the approach, choose tools, and spend time where it helps.
DFRU.description: You think through the goal and approach before choosing tools. You prefer to use existing tools for work they can handle and change the implementation route as needed. You weigh how to use limited time to solve important problems.
DFRU.inPractice: You may compare approaches, then combine existing tools around the actual goal.
DFRU.watchFor: A tool may fit the plan but have conditions you have not considered. Check them before depending on it.
DFRU.collaboration: Explain each tool's role and which parts would be affected if you replaced it later.

DFRA.name: Director
DFRA.summary: Start with an overall idea, then combine tools to build the design.
DFRA.description: You like forming an overall idea before choosing tools and modules. Tools can handle low-level details, but the combined code should express your design accurately. You care about clear connections and a consistent whole.
DFRA.inPractice: You may start with an overall idea and combine existing tools to build the design.
DFRA.watchFor: The combination you want may exceed what a tool supports. Check important extension interfaces early.
DFRA.collaboration: Show the overall design, then ask teammates to check how its parts connect.

DFEU.name: Doer
DFEU.summary: Try what works, change what doesn't, and focus on getting it done.
DFEU.description: You first ask whether the problem is solved. You try available tools and switch when they do not fit. You have little attachment to a language or technical approach; more time or complexity needs a practical return.
DFEU.inPractice: You may start with available tools, test a direct approach, and change it when it stops meeting the goal.
DFEU.watchFor: Frequent changes of approach can leave assumptions unexplained. Record the choices future maintainers need to know.
DFEU.collaboration: Show what works, explain what is still uncertain, and agree on what to test next.

DFEA.name: Explorer
DFEA.summary: Try different tools and let the experience reveal new possibilities.
DFEA.description: You enjoy trying different tools and often discover what you want to build after getting started. Unexpected discoveries can make you change direction. Alongside making the feature work, you care about how different combinations let you express ideas.
DFEA.inPractice: You may try different tools and combinations, then adjust the design based on what you discover.
DFEA.watchFor: Interesting experiments can distract from the goal. Set aside separate time for exploration and delivery.
DFEA.collaboration: Share discoveries early so teammates can help decide which direction deserves more time.

DGRU.name: Steward
DGRU.summary: Choose reliable tools and clear rules to make everyday work easier.
DGRU.description: You want reliable tools, clear rules and responsibilities, and a system that runs steadily. You prefer to leave routine details to the system and accept some constraints to reduce surprises and maintenance work.
DGRU.inPractice: You may choose a suitable platform, define operating rules, and let it handle routine work.
DGRU.watchFor: Stable defaults have limits. Check them again when requirements or dependencies change.
DGRU.collaboration: Clarify who maintains each mechanism and make the operating rules easy to find.

DGRA.name: Lawmaker
DGRA.summary: Think the rules through and let machines enforce them consistently.
DGRA.description: You want machines to enforce rules once they are clear. Types, frameworks, and automated checks can block invalid behavior and reduce reliance on people remembering what to do. You value consistent rules and prefer to limit the effect of individual improvisation on the system.
DGRA.inPractice: You may define the model and rules first, then use established tools to enforce them consistently.
DGRA.watchFor: Strict rules can make new requirements hard to express. Check whether the model still fits.
DGRA.collaboration: Explain each constraint and how teammates can propose and make changes to the rules.

DGEU.name: Administrator
DGEU.summary: Use established tools and real observations to keep solving problems reliably.
DGEU.description: You rely on mature tools and clear rules, then use tests and observations to check their reliability. When problems appear, you adjust configuration or switch approaches. Tools can handle internal details as long as they keep solving problems reliably.
DGEU.inPractice: You may test mature tools against actual needs and adjust configuration while keeping necessary guarantees.
DGEU.watchFor: New workloads can change system behavior. Keep tests close to actual operating conditions.
DGEU.collaboration: Share the measurements behind your choice and make clear who is responsible for configuration.

DGEA.name: Sound Engineer
DGEA.summary: Try and adjust until the parts have consistent interfaces and behavior.
DGEA.description: You want mature tools to follow shared rules and keep adjusting them through use. Their combined interfaces should be consistent, their behavior should feel natural, and their details should not conflict. You care about whether the parts form a coherent system.
DGEA.inPractice: You may use mature components and keep checking their interfaces so the combined system stays consistent.
DGEA.watchFor: Consistent details may require costly wrappers. Weigh the benefit against adding another layer.
DGEA.collaboration: Show where interfaces differ and agree on the rules the whole system should follow.

preferencePractice.C: You tend to keep control of key mechanisms. You might write module connections explicitly, configure operating policies yourself, or maintain a necessary library change.
preferencePractice.D: You tend to let suitable tools handle general mechanisms. Existing modules, supported plugins, or build platforms can leave more time for specific business problems.
preferencePractice.F: You tend to keep freedom to combine and adjust things. While requirements are changing, you might use objects with adjustable fields or configurable workflows and leave some checks until use.
preferencePractice.G: You tend to define allowed behavior upfront. You might separate result types, restrict API parameters, or list permitted state transitions.
preferencePractice.R: You tend to form an explanation before choosing a test. Following call chains, estimating costs, or reasoning through execution orders helps you decide what evidence to gather next.
preferencePractice.E: You tend to observe actual behavior before deeper analysis. After reproducing a problem, building a small prototype, or taking measurements, you decide what to investigate.
preferencePractice.U: You tend to invest when there is a practical need. New requirements, repeated edits, and migration costs influence when you refactor, extract a shared function, or preserve an existing API.
preferencePractice.A: You value the quality of concepts and expression themselves. You may spend extra time clarifying responsibilities, choosing precise names, and keeping internal implementations consistent.

questions.Q01: When two frameworks both meet my needs, I would prefer the one with an inspectable request-handling process, even if setup takes more steps.
questions.Q02: If an API can return success or failure, I would define separate result types so the code restricts the fields each can contain upfront.
questions.Q03: When a function returns an unexpected result, I would read along its call chain to infer where the problem might be before running a check.
questions.Q04: When code passes existing tests and has no evident maintenance problems, I would wait until it gets in the way of implementing a new requirement before considering refactoring.
questions.Q05: When a project must support several databases, I would prefer an existing data-access tool to handle their differences if it meets the requirements.
questions.Q06: In a small script with evolving requirements, I would prefer data objects that can gain fields as needed, with suitability checks when the fields are read.
questions.Q07: When a bug occurs intermittently, I would narrow the inputs and rerun the failing scenario before analyzing its cause.
questions.Q08: When two implementations can deliver the same feature, I would be willing to spend much more time on the one with clearer responsibilities and a more coherent structure.
questions.Q09: Even for a small reusable module, I would prefer a mature open-source library that meets my needs over implementing my own version.
questions.Q10: When writing linked data-processing functions, I would let callers choose the order and check at runtime whether each step can use the previous step’s output.
questions.Q11: If I am unsure which of two algorithms is faster, I would compare them on typical project data before deciding which to investigate further.
questions.Q12: After a feature works and its variable names are understandable, I would still spend time distinguishing the names of variables with similar but different meanings.
questions.Q13: If failed requests need automatic retries, I would prefer to set retry counts and intervals myself, even if a mature tool’s defaults meet the requirements.
questions.Q14: If an API has invocation modes that cannot be combined, I would use separate methods that each accept only the parameters for that mode.
questions.Q15: If a program with repeated loops and data queries slows down, I would estimate loop counts and per-query costs before deciding what to measure.
questions.Q16: For an internal tool used by a few colleagues, I would prefer instructions for their actual use and defer full documentation until its audience grows.
questions.Q17: When one internal behavior prevents a library from meeting my needs, I would be willing to maintain a modified version to control that behavior directly.
questions.Q18: If a task has pending, active, and completed states, I would list allowed transitions upfront and restrict its update method to those transitions.
questions.Q19: If storing API results could reduce repeated queries, I would work out how long to retain them and when updates should clear them before experimenting.
questions.Q20: Even when a business concept appears only once, I would be willing to give it its own class or module so it has a clear place in the code.
questions.Q21: If logs need custom information and an existing logging library’s extension interface supports it, I would use that interface and leave internal processing to the library.
questions.Q22: For a frequently changing experimental feature, I would prefer adjustable configuration options, with their combinations checked when the configuration is read.
questions.Q23: When evaluating a new framework, I would implement a small feature with it before reading the documentation in depth about specific issues.
questions.Q24: When similar code blocks are short and easy to change independently, I would prefer to keep them until repeated edits become burdensome before extracting a shared function.
questions.Q25: If an existing platform can compile, test, and package the code, I would let it arrange and maintain those steps.
questions.Q26: When data checks differ slightly across business contexts, I would prefer each call site to choose its checks and retain room for adjustment.
questions.Q27: When unsure how much data to process per batch, I would try several batch sizes and use timings and failures to identify a workable range.
questions.Q28: When an older API's naming is untidy but users understand it, I would prefer to keep it and avoid requiring callers to rename their usage.
questions.Q29: If a framework can discover and connect modules automatically, I would still state which module depends on which in code, even if that requires additional wiring.
questions.Q30: When adding operating modes to a tool, I would prefer to define allowed configurations for each mode upfront and reject other combinations during configuration checks.
questions.Q31: If two tasks might read and write the same data at the same time, I would sketch execution orders and infer conflict points before testing them.
questions.Q32: In code review, when two internal modules use different but understandable approaches, I would still want to spend time expressing the same logic consistently.
